articles.title: After Sea-Tac Arrests, Rally Organizers Call for ICE's Removal From Airports
paras: Video of masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting a father and daughter at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport over the weekend drew a response that reached beyond the airport: The Washington Indivisible Network announced a rally, Gov. Bob Ferguson called the agents' tactics "un-American," and activists pressed Ferguson over federal agents' access to state driver data .

The viral video shows several masked ICE agents pulling the father and daughter off a jet bridge on Nov. 21 as the daughter screams. The detained people were identified by friends and family as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter Sofia Hernandez Mejía. The pair were boarding an Alaska Airlines domestic flight to Los Angeles when masked agents arrested them.

Passengers boarding the same flight attempted to intervene, the video reveals, while at least one used a phone to film Mejía, asking her to state her name. Both Mejía and Mendoza were taken off the jetway by agents through a side door.
The father and daughter were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, their attorney Olia Catala told KIRO 7 .

Washington law generally bars law enforcement officers, including federal immigration agents, from wearing face coverings that conceal their identities during on-duty interactions with the public. A spokesperson for the state attorney general's office told RANGE Media that the office lacks authority to enforce the ban . But a person detained in violation of the law can sue for damages under certain conditions.

The rally is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. Nov. 24 at Angle Lake Park in SeaTac. Organizers, including local unions and Washington Indivisible, want ICE "removed from all our airports" and seek a limit on the "sharing of passenger data."

The Department of Homeland Security said they arrested Mejía and Mendoza because the pair overstayed their visas . Catala said that they have done " everything correctly " and have no criminal history, The Seattle Times reported.

In an interview with KUOW on Nov. 23, Gov. Bob Ferguson said that ICE operates without any transparency and added that the agency doesn't give Sea-Tac or Alaska Airlines any advance notice of actions. He described the ICE agents' conduct as "un-American, these masked guys running around without identifying themselves."
He said he was working with different organizations to help Mejía and Mendoza and has texted with a close friend of Mejía.

Ferguson said he's also met with Alaska Airlines representatives and suggested that the airline make a stronger statement about removing ICE from the airport. "They need to call on ICE to get out of the business" of doing what they're doing, he said.

Hours after the arrests, as the video ricocheted across social media, OneAmerica and MLK Labor held a joint press conference at the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 3000 office in Des Moines. Ferguson attended.

Throughout the press conference, audience members spoke up about ICE's access to driver data held by the Washington State Department of Licensing. Researchers at the University of Washington's Center for Human Rights documented 406 cases from August 2025 through Nov. 11, 2026, in which immigration arrests followed federal agents' searches of Washington license plate records through Nlets , a national data-sharing network.

An elementary school teacher who attended the press conference said they had witnessed the arrest of a coworker on school property. They questioned Ferguson about driver data, asking what more the state is doing to protect school safety. According to Ferguson, Washington state currently does everything within its power to keep ICE from accessing driver data.

"For data that the state has, ICE has been disconnected from all of it, including license plates. What happens, however, is other federal actors don't care what the rules are and get that information. We cut those individuals off each individual time that they do that," said Ferguson.
"The Trump administration and ICE are so annoyed by us cutting them off that we've been sued by the Trump administration," he added.

Ferguson also called for the abolition of ICE and its banishment from all airports, arguing that ICE is beyond reform. He said he would ask Alaska Airlines to request ICE have no presence at the airport. "And I'm going to be reaching out to every airline that operates out of Sea-Tac and [request] that statement be made to ICE," he said.

Following the press conference, three activists from Superfamilia KC , a grassroots organization that organizes mutual aid and advocates for King County's undocumented communities, entered the room with a bullhorn. They accused Ferguson of being complicit in ICE's continued use of DOL data to make arrests in Washington state. As attendees left the room, the activists chanted through a bullhorn that "the governor collaborates with ICE."
After the demonstration, Superfamilia KC posted a statement on its Instagram account that described the press conference as "performative."

articles.title: From dorm delivery robots to real‑world video games, UW students show off inventions
articles.author: Grace Kaste
paras: Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

“We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya said. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”

CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers . It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort , a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.
“We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu said. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”
One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

“The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya said. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”
According to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry said have changed everything.
“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry said.

Other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

“Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”

His team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

Other inventions sought to get users off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

“I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae said. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”
Also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.
“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev said. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”

His prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

“We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards said. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”
Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:

This cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

To do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.
“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat said. “Maybe even globally.”

articles.title: Tech Moves: AWS nabs Salesforce exec; former OpenAI employees launch Seattle startup; Portal hire
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Muralidhar Krishnaprasad has been named as vice president of analytics, storage and databases at Amazon Web Services , a role that reports to AWS CEO Matt Garman. Krishnaprasad, who goes by MK, left Salesforce after eight years. He was president and chief technology officer there, where he helped build the company’s agentic enterprise platform.
At AWS, he will lead an organization that unites Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), database and analytics services.
“MK brings deep technical roots, a customer-obsessed mindset and experience building data platforms at global scale,” Garman said in an email to staff.
Earlier in his career, MK spent more than a decade each at Oracle and Microsoft.

— After more than 13 years at Microsoft , Bonnie McCracken has been named VP of strategy and chief technology officer for communications. She is also general manager of innovation and thought leadership communications.

— Skye Scofield , Pablo Beltran and Brent Echols left OpenAI roughly two months ago to launch a Seattle startup that is currently in stealth mode. Scofield served as chief of staff to OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji, CTO of applications. Beltran and Echols, both software engineers, were members of the company’s technical staff.

More recently, Brandon Zinn joined the stealth startup as head of sales. All four overlapped in earlier roles at Statsig. In a post today on LinkedIn , Zinn asked for leads with home services owners “who could use help getting more work or making the business easier to run.”
The team is working with business owners in “roofing, tree care, plumbing, HVAC, painting, etc. Especially teams of 3–15 people where a lot still falls directly on the owner,” Zinn said.
Beltran said in a separate post that the startup has passed $100,000 in annual recurring revenue and is rapidly developing its software.

— Portal Space Systems , a Bothell, Wash.-based space company, has appointed Egbert Maben as principal satellite guidance, navigation and control (GNC) engineer — the startup’s first dedicated GNC hire. Last month, Portal reached Earth orbit for the second time this year.

Maben joined from Blue Origin, where he was a leader in GNC and hardware integration and helped resolve mission-critical hardware failures. He also tackled assembly, integration and test, a process that verifies the performance of software and hardware components. He previously spent nearly two decades at Lockheed Martin.

Maben, the company notes, has been keeping bees since ninth grade. “The only thing that’s left to see is whether Egbert, like bees, will be using dance to communicate those directives to our spacecraft,” Portal said on LinkedIn .

— Seattle-based Yoodli has named Jessica Evans as its first mid-market sales leader.The startup recently expanded from helping people practice speeches, sales pitches and job interviews to providing corporate training across a wide range of skills. Evans joins from ClickUp.
— PATH , a Seattle-based global health nonprofit, has appointed three new board members:

— Ian McAllister joined Boston-based Toast as vice president of Product, Video AI, in October after the restaurant software company acquired Airloom AI , the Seattle-area startup he founded and led as CEO. A longtime Seattle tech GM and product leader, he spent 12 years at Amazon and also held leadership roles at Airbnb and Uber.

McAllister said the idea for Airloom came when his wife, Sara McAllister , asked him to pick a security camera system for Allister , the Mercer Island restaurant and cocktail bar she owns and runs as GM. McAllister started Airloom AI to help restaurants use their existing video to improve the guest experience and operations. At Toast, he’ll continue that effort by combining Airloom’s technology with Toast’s platform. He’s building out Toast’s Vision AI team by hiring for multiple Seattle-based and remote product, engineering and AI/ML roles.

articles.title: Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported , citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported .

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.
“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the company’s earnings call last month.
Amazon announced the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO , ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role .

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips , mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.
Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition .

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported . Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes . The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.
The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported .
Amazon bought Annapurna , also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron , a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other big buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August , before it walked away in September . Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech , and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”
The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

articles.title: From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Since Grant Canary launched his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed , which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation .

The company recently shifted again, adding a new line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.
When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.
What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the issues.
What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.
If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.
What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally important: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.
Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.
In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.
What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.
What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.
What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

articles.title: Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey’
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.
But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.
“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.
A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.
Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”
He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”
Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”
Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.
Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project , according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.
Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.
Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage . He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.
(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs , Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.)
Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

articles.title: Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe , reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.
They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023 . In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft , where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.
GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.
“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.
The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.
Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.
Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.
“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.
Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation .

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.
Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.
He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.
He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

articles.title: Transit Advocates Push Larsen to Ditch Car-Centric 'BUILD America 250 Act'
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A Washington congressman is finding himself at the heart of one of the first major fights unfolding ahead of January's Democratic takeover in Congress, with billions of dollars in federal transportation funding on the line.

Among the many leadership positions about to change hands in Washington, the next chair of the House's Transportation and Infrastructure committee is very likely to be Rick Larsen. And Larsen, who represents Washington's 2nd Congressional District including Bellingham, Everett, and the San Juan Islands, is facing pressure from advocates to rethink plans to advance a transportation funding package he negotiated with Congressional Republicans earlier this year, known as the "BUILD America 250 Act."

The BUILD Act was rolled out in May, as a replacement for the expiring, Biden-era Investment in Infrastructure and Jobs Act (IIJA). At the time, Larsen touted the bill as investing $580 billion in "job-creating infrastructure," highlighting elements like a boost in federal funding for ferries.

But as the Bipartisan Policy Center noted at the time , the guaranteed funding levels in the bill would represent a decrease in federal support for public transit compared to the IIJA while at the same time boosting spending on highways.

Analysis from the Georgetown Climate Center concluded that full enactment of the BUILD Act would spike carbon emissions annually by 14 to 22 million metric tons, and lead to more than 1,000 additional road deaths due to a pivot away from safety infrastructure.

So the news that Larsen was planning to use the BUILD Act as the template for the next federal transportation package, in the wake of the largest electoral victory for Democrats since the 1970s was met with widespread alarm among those who follow federal transportation policy.

"We are not starting from scratch. We just don’t have the time to start from scratch, the capacity to start from scratch,” Larsen said in an interview with POLITICO earlier this month. "We have a good bill to start with."
Larsen added that committee members would likely insert additional items "that the Democrats would be more supportive of" while they "move some things around underneath the top line."

Larsen has a reputation for being pro-transit, regularly appearing at Sound Transit ribbon cuttings and referencing his past efforts to secure $1.8 billion in federal funding for Lynnwood Link in 2018. But with transportation funding not likely to get a significant amount of national attention compared to other issues tackled by a newly Democratic Congress, there are no assurances that the flaws in the BUILD America 250 Act are going to be fixed.
Transportation advocacy organizations have been pushing Larsen to fully ditch the BUILD Act, framing the recycling of the bill as a generational mistake.

"Incoming House leaders should not advance a bill that was produced with the help of so many members of Congress who just got sent home by their voters. And on the flip side, the huge influx of new members who were just sent to Washington should get their chance to craft a different approach to transportation—a new Congress should mean a new sheet of paper," Transportation for America's Steve Davis wrote in a blog post on November 6. "The dynamics have certainly changed. A better deal can be had. Congress should bury the BUILD Act and start over fresh."
An action alert to push Larsen has already generated more than 16,000 letters on the issue.

"The BUILD America 250 Act would commit the country to another five years of traffic, pollution, and expensive car dependence while leaving public transit systems without the funding they desperately need," that action alert from National Campaign for Justice noted.

The IIJA expired on September 30, with Congress approving a stopgap spending bill that slashed transit and rail spending that extended that deadline to December 11. Another extension is all but certain,

While future levels of transit spending remain an open question, Larsen will also be tasked with managing the fact that the Trump administration has been refusing to spend the transit funding that's already been approved. In a letter sent earlier this month to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and the Acting Director of the Federal Transit Administration (FTA), Larsen joined with Senators Patty Murray and Elizabeth Warren to call out "holding infrastructure dollars hostage," per a press release .
Murray is set to take the gavel in the powerful Senate Appropriations committee, putting her in the driver's seat on future federal transportation spending as well.

"[W]e have watched for months as FTA and OMB have stonewalled the progress of worthy transit projects," the letter stated. "Your agencies have neglected for a year to advance the Boston Green Line Transformation project and the Los Angeles Southeast Gateway Line to the [Capital Investment Grant] Engineering phase under current program rules that were adopted in November of 2025 – without any justification or explanation for the delay."

While no Seattle-area transit projects were referenced in the letter, Sound Transit is counting on FTA dollars as it moves toward construction on the West Seattle and Tacoma Dome Link Extension projects, with a failure to secure those grants likely having cascading impacts on a financially strained system expansion plan that already took a big hit earlier this year . Meanwhile, the Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) for the Ballard Link Extension has been held up by federal review for over a year, only now being released on December 11.

For its part, King County Metro announced this summer it was no longer seeking federal funding for its RapidRide R Line enhanced bus project, preferring to go it alone. Officials framed defederalizing funding as speeding up project delivery given the run around the FTA has given many transit projects. Metro is still counting on federal funding for its RapidRide K Line , which will run between Kirkland's Totem Lake and Eastgate in Bellevue.

The federal threats to transit funding don't stop there. Earlier this fall, FTA advanced a rule change that would revamp eligibility criteria on one of its biggest transit grant programs, making it harder for projects to qualify – and apply retroactively to projects already in the pipeline. If implemented, that would scale back federal transit funding even further, shifting costs back onto transit agencies that aren't prepared to shoulder the burden.

“The new guidance is a part of the Trump administration’s systematic campaign to reduce or eliminate funding for new transit projects,” Yonah Freemark, principal research associate at the Urban Institute, told Streetsblog . “It’s basically a crisis for transit agencies.”

Washington's congressional delegation, including Larsen and Murray, is set to be put in a prime position to be able to help confront that crisis, but it remains to be seen whether that's going to be enough to resist a full-out federal assault on sustainable transportation options including public transit.

articles.title: Harry’s Fine Foods: 10 years of community on Bellevue Ave E — and the roots of its food+drink family’s next leap inside a $4.9M+ Capitol Hill mansion
articles.author: Anne Jorgenson
paras: Renovations underway before Harry’s 2016 debut (Image: Harry’s Fine Foods)
Ten years ago, Julian Hagood was simultaneously working and running his own catering business out of his shared apartment in Capitol Hill. As orders grew, so did the need for a home for the business.

“Knowing that I’ve wanted to be a chef since I was 10 years old, it was always kind of my dream to have my own space and give people my idea of hospitality,” said Hagood. As a neighborhood resident Hagood was familiar with the area, and when the space availed itself, he jumped on the opportunity.
“Seeing the vision for it and what it could possibly be was an exciting thing,” reminisced Hagood.

Named after the corner store that once occupied the space, Harry’s Fine Foods has always strived to be a local watering hole. Their ten-year anniversary celebrates both the accomplishment of a decade and the community that has made the independent restaurant run by a husband and husband team successful.
Surviving, if not always thriving, the restaurant has weathered the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and rising operational costs, a feat not lost on Hagood and Jake Santelli .
“As the brand recognition of Harry’s has grown, Fine Foods has grown beyond being just a neighborhood restaurant, but I don’t think it’s ever lost its connection to the neighborhood,” said Santelli.

All under the umbrella of the Harry’s Good Times hospitality family, the business has now expanded to four establishments: Harry’s Fine Foods and Harry’s Guest House on Bellevue Ave, Harry’s Beach House on Alki, and upcoming The Baillie on 14th Ave E near Volunteer Park –their most ambitious project yet.
Plans for The Baillie are taking shape at 14th and Aloha

Set to open in late 2027, The Baillie will be a boutique hotel and restaurant on Millionaire’s Row , inside a renovated 113-year-old mansion. Hagood and Santelli plan to make the Baillie a place for both visitors and the neighborhood.
Part hotel, part restaurant, part lounge, The Baillie will maintain space for first, come first served neighborhood patrons.

“We’ve lost spontaneity in the dining experience. The thing that is the proper defining feature of a neighborhood restaurant is that no matter what you don’t need a reservation, you’re going to show up and we’re going to make sure we feed you,” said Santelli.

The couple purchased the historic 11,000-square-foot bed-and-breakfast in February for $4.9 million, and plan to operate seven days a week once opened, welcoming visitors to the neighborhood, be they tourists, passersby, or parents who managed to find a babysitter and want to enjoy a night out.
“We’re all so busy in our lives and work, we’re designing the space in a way that you can make a night of it with the Baillie,” said Santelli.

Taking on the project is a major financial undertaking but the dollars will be nearly eclipsed by the paperwork and navigating the city’s zoning and business laws. Challenges like sorting out how to remain open past 10 PM in this residential area of Capitol Hill will be part of what makes The Baillie special — just like the original Harry’s.
That hospitality mindset is the ethos of Harry’s Good Times, and all of that started with Harry’s Fine Foods in the fall of 2016 .

“What we try and do is just give people a reason to come and see us again. Ideally that will help us – be the best restaurant, be the best operator, be the kindest,” said Santelli. “That’s why we call it Harry’s Good Times — you cannot forget to find joy even when things are going crazy. It’s the best way to get through your life.”

None of this is to say everything has been sunshine and roses, but the couple says they operate with a glass half full mindset. As business costs increase citywide, Hagood and Santelli know that the team and the customers behind Harry’s Fine Foods is what keeps the dream alive.
“We’re not going anywhere, we will always be rooted in that neighborhood mentality.”
That mindset is important to the city right now, especially for independent businesses.

A 2026 Business Climate Survey by the Seattle Metro Chamber and Downtown Seattle Association shows that a majority of restaurants believe that the city’s business climate has worsened over the last year and are pessimistic about the next 12 months.
Along with thanks to the community for the last ten years, Hagood’s parting words were a call to action.
“Go visit your neighborhood restaurants because if you don’t they may not be around much longer — not just Harry’s.”
Harry’s Fine Foods is located at 601 Bellevue Ave E. Learn more at harrysfinefoods.com .

articles.title: Mayor Wilson celebrates ‘Our New Progressive Majority,’ incoming council member in anniversary address
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Marking the one-year anniversary of her election win , Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson released a video address celebrating a growing progressive coalition at Seattle City Hall and across the nation, spotlighting the arrival of incoming District 5 Councilmember Nilu Jenks as a pivotal boost for her administration’s agenda.

In her “ Our New Progressive Majority ” address, Wilson framed recent election wins across the nation and in Seattle as a mandate from residents frustrated by homelessness and the rising cost of living. Locally, the centerpiece of that shift is Jenks, the newly elected D5 representative Wilson described as “a pragmatic progressive with whom I’m so excited to work on the Seattle City Council.”

Jenks, who defeated opponent Julie Kang in the November election to represent North Seattle’s District 5, adds a key ally for Wilson’s push on affordable housing, pedestrian safety, and expanded transit. Wilson noted that voters nationwide echoed Seattle’s demand for leadership that will “deliver policies and programs that materially improve people’s lives”.

With Jenks joining the council, Wilson said she will aim to build on her administration’s first-year legislative record, which includes banning rental “junk fees,” fast-tracking shelter expansion, guaranteeing free school meals, and passing a major public transit funding measure. However, the mayor cautioned that governing requires balancing bold progressive ideals with pragmatic execution, pointing to her recent veto of an RV permitting system and her decision to move forward with police CCTV cameras following a privacy audit.

“The big bold progressive initiatives that make headlines need to pass this test, and so does the mundane work of city government — making sure the lights stay on and the potholes get filled,” Wilson said as she urged the new wave of progressive officials to focus on tangible daily results.

articles.title: NATO witnesses a surge of airspace violations by Russia as Moscow seeks to test alliance
articles.author:
<name>Frederic Lemieux, Professor of the Practice and Faculty Director of the Master's in Applied Intelligence, Georgetown University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/frederic-lemieux-147315"/>
paras: NATO convened an urgent meeting on Nov. 23, 2026 , to discuss the violation of members’ airspace by Russia.

It follows an incident three days earlier in which three objects – believed to be two missiles and a drone – crashed in Poland in what the country’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, described as an “intentional provocation” by Russia . If true, it would be far from the first such testing of the airspace of a NATO country.

Russian aircraft, drones and missiles have violated NATO airspace dozens of times since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. And while individually, many of these incidents appear minor – a drone crash here, a brief fighter incursion there, a missile discovered only after the fact – taken together, I believe the numbers tell a far more troubling story.
To get a full picture of the scale of violations, I conducted a systematic review of Russian airspace violations against NATO members ) from 2022 through the end of November.

It reveals not just an increase but a sharp acceleration accompanied by rising severity and widening geographic scope. In 2026, through Nov. 20, NATO members recorded 25 attributed Russian airspace violations – more than four times as many as in 2024 and 43% of all incidents recorded over the five-year period.
This has not been a gradual escalation; it was a dramatic change.

I identified airspace violations through a systematic review of international news media coverage, corroborated with official NATO press releases and cross-validated against operational assessments and geospatial reporting from the Institute for the Study of War .
Included were violations of airspace by drones heavily suspected to be Russian but that could not be 100% confirmed.

Between 2022 and 2024, the annual number of violations rose steadily but modestly. There were four incidents in 2022, five in 2023 and six in 2024. That corresponds to year-on-year increases of roughly 25% and 20%.
In 2025, the count jumped to 18, a 200% increase in a single year. And that pace has continued into 2026.

Such a surge is statistically and strategically significant. It strongly suggests that Russian airspace violations are no longer episodic spillovers from the war in Ukraine, but part of a sustained pattern of pressure directed at NATO itself. The 2026 figures reinforce this: The count has kept rising even after the 2025 surge.
The character of these incidents has also changed.

In 2022, all four violations were what I classify as low-intensity events: brief incursions into Swedish airspace by Russian fighters, the crash of an Orlan-10 reconnaissance drone in Romania and the later discovery of a Russian cruise missile in Poland. These incidents were serious but short-lived and geographically limited.

By 2023, violations had become more repetitive. Romania alone experienced multiple drone incursions and debris discoveries over several months, often triggering fighter scrambles. All five incidents that year fell into a midrange severity category: more persistent than before but still largely confined to border regions.

The transition toward higher-intensity incursions became clearer in 2024. Of the six violations that year, half involved high-severity characteristics such as deeper penetration of a NATO country or broader geographic exposure. A Russian cruise missile crossed into Polish airspace , drones entered Romania on multiple consecutive nights, and a Russian drone crashed well inside Latvian territory . These incidents expanded both the depth and the geographic footprint of violations.

Then came 2025. Of the 18 violations recorded that year , a clear majority qualify as high-severity events. These include a Russian drone that penetrated nearly 60 miles (100 kilometers) into Polish territory before crashing near Osiny without prior radar detection; a drone that remained inside Romanian airspace for approximately four hours, crossing multiple counties before crashing in Vaslui; and a massive 21-drone swarm over Poland on Sept. 9-10 that forced the closure of major civilian airports in Warsaw, Rzeszów and Lublin.

Manned aircraft also returned in force. Russian MiG-31 interceptors flew over Estonia for about 12 minutes with transponders – onboard devices that automatically respond to radar signals by transmitting an aircraft’s identity and altitude, enabling air traffic control and air defense systems to track it – switched off.
In October, a Russian Su-30 fighter accompanied by an Il-78 refueling tanker violated Lithuanian airspace – an unmistakable signal of endurance and deliberate mission planning.
In December 2025, suspected Russian drones were shot down and later recovered in Turkey on multiple dates, indicating a persistent provocation rather than a one-off incursion.

Perhaps most strikingly, Western Europe was seemingly no longer exempt. On Dec. 4, 2025, five unidentified drones flew over France’s Île Longue naval base , home to the country’s nuclear ballistic missile submarines. French personnel reportedly fired at the suspected Russian drones.
Just weeks later, on Christmas Day, Polish fighters intercepted a Russian reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea.

In 2026, the incidents grew more dangerous. In May, a Russian drone struck an apartment block in Galați, Romania , injuring two people, the first civilian injuries on NATO soil from such an incursion. Then on July 30, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile flew roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) into Poland before exploding in a field near Lublin. On Nov. 20, during a mass Russian strike on Ukraine, a Kh-101, likely a second missile and a jet-powered drone entered Polish airspace .

Manned aircraft also crossed into NATO airspace. A Russian Su-30 fighter entered Estonian airspace in March with no flight plan and no contact with air traffic control, and in September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad into Poland .

Severity and frequency are not the only dimensions that changed. Geographical reach has, too. In 2022, Russian violations affected three NATO members. By 2024, that number had grown to four. In 2025, it expanded to six: Romania, Poland, Estonia, Lithuania, Turkey and France. In 2026, the violations attributed to Russia have so far been concentrated in four members – Romania, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania – with Romania alone accounting for 20 of the 25. Romania’s defense ministry counted 35 unauthorized drone entries by mid-October, many too brief to be reported individually.
Pressure was applied simultaneously in the Black Sea region, the Baltic states and Western Europe.

This widening scope matters because it undermines the idea that these incidents are localized accidents. Instead, they resemble a distributed pattern of Russia probing across NATO’s eastern and southern flanks and into its strategic core. The narrower footprint in 2026 does not signal de-escalation. The pressure has instead concentrated along the flank that borders the war, and it has grown more dangerous there. NATO’s political response reflects this shift. For the first time since the war began, members invoked Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty , the mechanism for collective consultation when a member feels its security is threatened.

Poland did so after the September 2025 drone swarm, and Estonia followed after the MiG-31 incursion later that month. Although only two of the 18 incidents triggered Article 4, their timing is revealing: No such invocations occurred in the previous three years combined.

In 2026, no member has invoked Article 4 so far, even after a Russian cruise missile flew deep into Poland in July. Instead, allies have shifted from tolerance to engagement: Romanian F-16s and allied jets have shot down six Russian drones over Romania , and Italian Eurofighters destroyed an armed Russian drone over Lithuania in September.

From a strategic standpoint, the danger lies less in any single violation than in their cumulative effect. Airspace incursions sit in a gray zone between peace and open conflict. They impose operational and psychological costs, test air defense systems and provide valuable intelligence on NATO’s detection thresholds and response times, all while staying below the legal threshold of armed attack.

The data from 2025 and 2026 shows that this gray-zone activity has intensified dramatically. A threefold increase in 2025, followed by a further rise in 2026, coupled with a shift toward deeper, longer and more disruptive incidents across multiple theaters, points to a deliberate campaign rather than accidental spillover.

For NATO, the implication is clear. Monitoring individual incidents is no longer sufficient. What now matters is the rate of acceleration, the severity profile and the geographic dispersion of violations. If current trends persist as the war in Ukraine enters its fifth year, the alliance’s greatest challenge may not be responding to a single dramatic breach but managing the mounting pressure created by many smaller ones – each calibrated to test resolve without triggering open conflict.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously
articles.author:
<name>Michael Nalick, Assistant Professor of Management, University of Denver</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/michael-nalick-2487414"/>
paras: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.

This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit.

Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump , who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated.

As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something.

CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization.

But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent.

One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows.

One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.

Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well.
In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it.

In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks .

Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.
My research has found that risk to be high.

When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first.

Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.

Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.

In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?
In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”
Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake.

CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.

Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.

It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.

In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.

The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct.

It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted : “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.”
This article was updated on Nov. 23, 2026, to reflect Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO.

articles.title: What was the first animal that ever lived on Earth?
articles.author:
<name>Matthew W. Brown, Dr. Donald L. Hall Professor of Biology, Mississippi State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/matthew-w-brown-693109"/>
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
What was the first animal on Earth? – Keira, age 10, Eugene, Oregon, and Julian, age 7, South Bend, Indiana
Imagine climbing into a time machine and setting the dial for when the very first animal was alive. You would need to travel really, really far back in time.

You would blow past the dinosaurs, which showed up about 230 million years ago . Keep going and you’d pass coil-shelled ammonites that swam in the oceans starting 450 million years ago, and then trilobites , armored animals that scuttled across the seafloor more than 520 million years ago. Further still, around 558 million years ago, you would meet Dickinsonia , a tiny, flat, ribbed oval only a few millimeters thick that looks more like a squashed pancake than any animal you know.
And even Dickinsonia was almost certainly not the first animal.
We are biologists who study single-celled life called protists . How complex life such as human beings showed up in the first place is one of the major questions in our field.
Honestly, nobody can name the first animal, but there are many clues about what it was probably like.
If we asked you what an animal is, you might say something that moves, eats and reproduces. The trouble is that plenty of nonanimals do all three.
For instance, single-celled amoebae crawl, hunt and swallow their prey whole – and they are not animals at all!

Biologists define an animal as an organism made of many cells that stick together, communicate and divide up the work of growing, eating and moving. Different types of cells specialize to do different jobs, and they all work together as one organism. And when animals eat, they take in outside material instead of making their own food from sunlight the way plants do.
Notice what is not on that list: Legs. Eyes. A brain. A mouth. That matters for what comes next.

SpongeBob SquarePants is a cartoon version of a real animal, the sea sponge . Real sponges do not wear square pants; they don’t even move around. They sit anchored to the seafloor, pumping seawater through thousands of tiny holes and straining out bacteria to eat. They have no brain, no heart and no muscles .

But sponges are still animals, and scientists often think of them as the simplest ones. Part of what makes them so interesting is a type of cell they have called choanocytes . Each choanocyte has a whiplike tail ringed by tiny fingerlike projections that trap food.

Choanocytes look almost exactly like choanoflagellates , free-living, single-celled organisms that are the closest living relatives of animals . Watching a colony of choanoflagellates feed together is about as close as you can get to seeing the doorway between single-celled life and animal life.

Imagine climbing down the animal tree of life going backward in time. You can start with animals alive today, which would be the leaves of the tree. Branches join where you encounter ancestors shared by different groups. Follow them far enough, and they all meet at a common ancestor of living animals . Scientists disagree about which groups belong on each side of that deepest branching point.

Some studies put sponges alone on one side of that fork , with every other living animal group, including us, on the other. Other studies put comb jellies in that position . In that case, these shimmering, jellylike ocean swimmers would occupy one side, while sponges and all other animals would occupy the other. This is what scientists mean when they describe either group as having “branched off first.”

It is important to remember that “branched off first” does not mean “unchanged.” Sponges, comb jellies and humans have all been evolving for the same amount of time , since our shared ancestor lived. Each lineage has followed its own evolutionary path, which over time has led to the great diversity of animals we see today, such as worms, insects, crabs and primates. Today’s sponges and comb jellies may therefore look very different from that common ancestor, making it difficult to picture what the first animal looked like.
Comparative biology can take us only so far.

Fossils are another source of information, but they show just a very narrow window into the past. Fossilization turns living material into stone , a process that works far better on hard parts such as shells, teeth and bones than on soft, squishy bodies. Because early animals were probably soft and small, they were likely easily erased from the record.

Also, fossilization works better in some kinds of environments than others. For example, muddy lake bottoms can bury dead organisms, protecting their remains from rapid decay so they have time to fossilize; any remains on wave-battered shores may wash away before they can fossilize.

Another line of evidence now available to scientists is genetic information. Genes, encoded in DNA strands inside every living organism, provide an instruction manual for how to build that creature. Cells copy that DNA and pass it on – a process that’s been going on for billions of years, generation after generation.

This genetic information accumulates slight changes over time, which scientists call mutations. It is the very existence of mutations that allows evolution – how life changes over time – to happen. This process is what generated the diversity of life you see today.

By studying the structure and architecture of DNA, as well as how it gets passed along, scientists can mathematically assemble family trees that extend very deep into the past. These family trees can help scientists make surprisingly good guesses about when and where an animal first arose. A creature’s genes hint at what it could possibly do.
Biologist Iñaki Ruiz-Trillo and his colleagues use a smartphone analogy that we find particularly useful when talking about the origin of animals.
A smartphone was not invented from scratch. Cameras, telephones, computers and the internet were all invented separately first. The innovation was combining them into a single piece of equipment.

Animals may have evolved in a similar way. Genes for sticking cells together, for sending signals between cells, for sensing the environment and for switching other genes on and off were already present in our single-celled relatives. Becoming an animal meant assembling that tool kit into one cooperating body.

The first animal was probably something very small, soft and unremarkable in an ancient ocean . It probably evolved over 650 million years ago. It certainly had different kinds of cells that were stuck together, doing specialized jobs.

Scientists may never be able to pinpoint the first animal, and we have a hard time trying to imagine it. But we do know that many of the cellular and molecular tools that helped early animal cells work together are still at work in your body today.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.
