articles.title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides
articles.author:
<name>Sofia Aman, PhD Researcher in Materials Science and Engineering, Northwestern University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sofia-aman-2769531"/>
paras: Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They’re entirely undeterred by the radiation – in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

The same type of species , Cladosporium sphaerospermum , has grown on the International Space Station, about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the surface of the Earth, in an experiment to test its resistance to radiation. Scientists found that it appeared to block a small amount of incoming radiation, and part of why comes down to a pigment called melanin.

I used to think of melanin the way most people do – as a pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their color. That changed early in my Ph.D. research when I read a 2019 study from the materials science lab I was joining that described how to make a fungal form of melanin in the lab. I was surprised by where this pigment shows up in nature, including in fungi growing at Chernobyl.

Melanin comprises a family of pigments. The melanin in human skin, called eumelanin, is built from nitrogen-containing building blocks. The melanin in many fungi, called allomelanin, is built from a different, nitrogen-free building block. That difference in structure gives it some unusual properties.

Scientists think allomelanin is a large part of why these fungi can live in such places. Over the course of my doctoral research, I learned that melanin does much more than add color. It holds onto metals, absorbs ultraviolet light, converts light into heat and helps produce the colors of some bird feathers.

Allomelanin has another remarkable property. My colleagues showed in 2021 that lab-made allomelanin is full of built-in pores, each less than a billionth of a meter wide. Chemists call these pores “intrinsic pores” because they are part of the material’s natural structure, rather than etched in later. To our knowledge, it is the only type of melanin with built-in porosity.

These nanometer-wide pores let the pigment act like a sponge for small molecules, including toxic ones , a feature we confirmed holds true whether the allomelanin comes directly from natural fungi or whether it is synthesized in our lab.
In a recent study published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal ACS Nano, my colleagues and I asked whether this material could do more than trap toxic chemicals. Could it also break them down?

Nerve agents such as sarin and VX belong to a group of chemicals called organophosphorus compounds . They block an enzyme the body uses to switch off nerve signals. Without that enzyme, nerves keep firing continuously, and a large enough exposure can turn lethal within minutes.

Chemical weapons are banned under international law, but they remain a persistent security concern. In May 2026, inspectors from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reported discovering dozens of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria left over from the Assad government.

Many pesticides used on agricultural crops rely on this exact same underlying chemistry. A 2026 analysis estimated that accidental pesticide poisonings number in the hundreds of millions each year, resulting in roughly 11,000 deaths annually around the world. Farmworkers operating with minimal protective gear face the greatest ongoing risk.

Today’s protective suits mostly rely on materials like activated carbon, which trap the chemicals but don’t break them down. Soldiers and farmworkers could benefit from protective gear that does more than block these toxic chemicals. Researchers, including my colleagues, are working on materials that could neutralize them as well.

Allomelanin on its own holds on to these organophosphorus molecules but leaves them chemically intact. A contaminated glove or mask that has merely trapped these toxins would remain hazardous to handle.

To improve our sponge, my colleagues and I made allomelanin in the form of tiny spheres, each hundreds of times narrower than a human hair. We then added tiny clusters made of a metal called zirconium . Each cluster consists of six zirconium atoms anchored by oxygen – it looks like a tiny cage of zirconium held together by oxygen.

Similar zirconium clusters form the active core of metal-organic frameworks , which are among the most studied materials for degrading chemical weapons. These clusters act like molecular scissors: When exposed to ambient moisture, they snip the chemical bonds holding organophosphates together, splitting them into less harmful pieces.
We tested different ways to attach these metal clusters to our synthetic allomelanin particles, ensuring the molecular scissors sat right where incoming toxins would land.

For safety, we tested the particles with a chemical stand-in widely used in research laboratories. It mimics nerve agents but carries far less toxicity. Our best-performing versions broke down half of the target chemical in less than 10 minutes, using only a tiny amount of zirconium. The particles kept working over several rounds of use, with very little metal leaking out.

Allomelanin’s built-in pores turned out to be essential. When we added the same zirconium clusters to other melanin-like materials without pores, they barely facilitated the breakdown. Adding too much zirconium also slowed the reaction, likely because more clusters clogged up the pores that water and toxic molecules needed to travel through. The best results came from balancing the amount of metal with open pore space.
This reaction usually needs alkaline conditions , which have a high pH and are the opposite of acidic – for example, baking soda dissolved in water is alkaline.

Water alone breaks down the trapped molecules far too slowly, over weeks or months. Alkaline conditions supply hydroxide, a negatively charged relative of water that is drawn to the molecule’s most dangerous bond and helps the zirconium snap it in minutes. In the lab, that means we add a liquid chemical to make the conditions alkaline, but doing so isn’t practical for a soldier’s jacket or a farmworker’s mask. Instead, we attached alkaline chemical groups directly to the particle surfaces.

We then took advantage of another property of melanin: It absorbs light and turns it into heat. Under a bright lamp for five minutes, the particles broke down about 10 times more of the stand-in chemical than they did in the dark. Simply heating the samples in the dark had a much smaller effect, which suggests light does more than warm the particles.

Our work has important limits. We tested a chemical surrogate in laboratory vials rather than using live nerve agents or agricultural pesticides floating in the air. We also have not yet woven these particles into commercial textiles. Our immediate next steps are to evaluate the material against the specific pesticides farmworkers encounter daily and to refine the particle coating process.

Getting the material into fabrics may be more straightforward than it sounds. Synthetic melanin naturally adheres to textile fibers without needing chemical glues, and our research group has previously demonstrated that synthetic melanins could act as sustainable fabric dyes.

In the future, we hope this work can help develop lightweight gloves, masks and uniforms that continuously destroy toxic chemicals on contact as people work in the sun. Zirconium is a common and relatively inexpensive metal, and each particle uses only a small amount, though we haven’t evaluated what the cost of making these materials at a larger scale could be.
More broadly, this study highlights the untapped potential of natural materials. Fungi spent millions of years evolving pigments to endure some of the harshest environments on Earth.
I started my Ph.D. thinking of melanin simply as a biological colorant. I now see it as a versatile, multifunctional material whose full capabilities we are only beginning to unlock.

articles.title: The University of Florida revives the ‘Gator bait’ cheer, reversing a ban over its troubling history
articles.author:
<name>Mark V. Barrow, Jr., Professor of History, Virginia Tech</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mark-v-barrow-jr-2726999"/>
paras: The sold-out crowd at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium , better known as “The Swamp,” roared with excitement as the University of Florida revived its “Gator bait” cheer at its 2026 season opener.

When the marching band played the familiar cue, thousands of fans responded with the “Gator chomp,” raising their outstretched arms and repeatedly opening and closing their hands like alligator jaws while shouting “Gator bait!”

The decision to bring back the popular cheer reversed a ban imposed in 2020 by University of Florida President Kent Fuchs, who was concerned about its racist origins amid the nationwide reckoning over race that followed the murder of George Floyd.

Current university president Stuart Bell remarked in an interview prior to his official appointment that “traditions matter” and suggested that the cheer could return because it remained “meaningful to the Gator family .” Since then, the university has restored the cheer, though it has not publicly identified who formally authorized its return .

The controversy surrounding this chant has often been framed narrowly by its supporters as a dispute over tradition versus political correctness. However, it raises important questions about whether a public university should continue to embrace a tradition that risks making some students and alumni feel less welcome on campus .

As an environmental and cultural historian and author of “ Gator!: The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, from First Encounters to Florida Man ,” I’ve spent years researching how alligators became intertwined with ideas about race, nature and Southern identity. My research points to a deeper history largely absent from the public debate over the cheer.

The roots of the “alligator bait” trope stretch back to the 18th century, when French explorers in North America claimed that a “ certain exhalation ” given off from Black skin attracted the voracious reptiles.
White plantation owners eagerly took up this racist theory because it discouraged enslaved people from fleeing into Southern swamps and marshes, where pursuing runaways was often difficult.

After the Civil War, as formerly enslaved people sought economic, educational and political advancement, many white Americans responded with efforts to reassert white supremacy . Alongside disenfranchisement , Jim Crow segregation and racial terrorism , they promoted stereotypes that demeaned and dehumanized African Americans .

One of these racist stereotypes was the depiction of Black Americans, especially children, as natural prey for alligators. Though it operated through images and ideas rather than physical force, the stereotype reinforced beliefs in Black inferiority. It also helped justify the intimidation, exclusion and violence that African Americans routinely faced during this period.

It was in this context that the racial slur “alligator bait” began circulating widely in the late 19th century. A bestselling photograph bearing that title, published in 1897, helped popularize the slur. Although the composite image of nine naked African American toddlers did not include an actual alligator, its title invited viewers to imagine Black children as special targets of the reptile.

The epithet soon spread through newspapers , postcards , editorial cartoons , songs and films . Ostensibly humorous images of alligators threatening or consuming Black Americans, especially children, also circulated widely across the U.S.

Whether Black children were ever actually used as bait to hunt alligators remains a subject of historical debate . But what is beyond dispute is that these images helped entrench degrading associations between African Americans and alligators in American popular culture for decades.

As the phrase alligator bait gained currency across the United States, it also began appearing in a new setting: University of Florida football games. The earliest published reference to the cheer seems to be a 1939 newspaper account of a home game against Georgia Tech.

When Georgia Tech’s Yellow Jackets took the field, Florida students taunted the all-white team with cries of “alligator bait.” Georgia Tech’s coach used the insult to motivate his players, asking whether they could imagine “anything lower than that.”

While it is impossible to know precisely how everyone present understood the phrase, it entered Florida football culture at a time when “alligator bait” remained a recognizable racial slur . By the late 1940s, the shortened form, “Gator bait,” which was both easier to chant and more closely aligned with the university’s “Gators” nickname, had become a regular fixture at Florida football games .

The cheer remained firmly embedded in campus culture as the university navigated the slow and often contentious process of desegregation. Like most Southern universities , the University of Florida resisted admitting Black students, enrolling its first African American law student , George H. Starke, only after a court order in 1958. The first Black undergraduates arrived four years later , and the football team remained segregated until 1968 .

Desegregation did not immediately transform the broader campus culture. The university continued to embrace traditions that celebrated the Confederacy and romanticized the Old South. In 1962, football coach Ray Graves placed decals of the Confederate battle flag on his players’ helmets before the Gator Bowl .

As late as the 1970s, the all-white Kappa Alpha fraternity continued a decades-long tradition of staging an annual “Old South” weekend that featured students parading in Confederate uniforms. In the 1950s and 1960s, that celebration even included a mock execution of Union General William T. Sherman and a secession proclamation .

When the student newspaper surveyed the campus in 1968 about whether to continue playing “Dixie” – the unofficial anthem of the Confederate States of America – at football games, 83% of students supported the practice. But the majority of Black students surveyed opposed it. “Dixie” remained a game-day staple until 1973 .

By the late 20th century, most Florida fans no longer understood “Gator bait” through the lens of Jim Crow-era racial stereotypes. Decades of use at football games had transformed the chant into a symbol of school spirit and athletic success.

No individual played a larger role in that transformation than Lawrence Wright, the hard-hitting safety who helped lead Florida to its first national championship. Wright, who is African American, did not invent the cheer, as is often claimed , but he helped elevate it to iconic status. Following Florida’s victory over rival Florida State in 1995, he famously rallied fans with the refrain , “If you ain’t a Gator, you must be Gator bait.”

When the Gators became national champions the next season , the chant became even more deeply enshrined in Florida football culture. For most fans, “Gator bait” came to symbolize pride in the university rather than anything connected to the phrase’s earlier racist history.
While most fans were unaware of it, “alligator bait” remained a documented racial slur , creating a tension between the phrase’s historical origins and its modern meaning.

That tension came to a head in 2020, when Fuchs suspended the cheer amid a broader university effort to address racism and inequity. While acknowledging that he knew of “no evidence of racism associated with our ‘Gator Bait’ cheer at UF sporting events,” Fuchs argued that the phrase’s “horrific historic racist imagery” warranted its retirement.

Critics, including Wright, responded that the cheer’s meaning at Florida had become detached from those historical associations . “Gator bait” was a cherished university tradition, they argued , neither generally understood nor intended as racist.
Six years later, under Bell, the university has reinstated the cheer amid a political and cultural climate markedly different from the one that had prompted its suspension.

Still, I believe the debate surrounding its return reveals that the controversy has never simply been about political correctness or school spirit. In my view, it is also about how institutions reckon with difficult histories and whether traditions can be separated from the historical meanings that gave rise to them.
Even if most fans today understand the cheer as an expression of school spirit, universities do not simply inherit traditions. They choose which ones they wish to preserve, modify or discard.

Whether the university made the right decision is open to debate. What is not in dispute is that the “Gator bait” cheer emerged during a period when “alligator bait” functioned as a racial slur and the University of Florida excluded Black students while embracing traditions that celebrated the Confederacy.
The Conversation reached out to the university, and it declined to add to Bell’s previous comments on this matter.

articles.title: Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?
articles.author:
<name>Karen Stollznow, Senior Research Fellow of Linguistics, University of Colorado Boulder; Griffith University; University of New England</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/karen-stollznow-890330"/>
paras: Roughly half of the world’s population speaks more than one language. But speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.

Throughout history, various people have attracted attention for their remarkable linguistic abilities . Some have genuinely mastered numerous languages, while others have exaggerated their proficiency or struggled to demonstrate their purported abilities.

In my 2026 book “ Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language ,” I explore the science of language, including how people acquire, understand and use it, from childhood language development to learning additional languages.

The word polyglot comes from the Greek word polyglōttos , meaning “many-tongued.” It describes someone who speaks multiple languages, but it leaves some important questions unanswered: How many languages must someone know, and how proficient must they be, to earn the title?

In the 1998 edition of the “Guinness Book of World Records,” Ziad Youssef Fazah was named the world’s greatest living polyglot . Born in Liberia and raised speaking Arabic, Fazah claimed to speak, read and understand an astonishing 59 languages. At the time, The Washington Post dubbed him the “One-man Tower of Babel.”
He was hardly the first person to attract attention for his supposed extraordinary linguistic abilities.
Cardinal Giuseppe Mezzofanti, an Italian scholar born in 1774, was reportedly proficient in 38 languages.

The 10th-century philosopher Al-Farabi was said to know 70 languages, while the 19th-century German linguist Hans Conon von der Gabelentz was believed to know 80 languages , according to accounts of his linguistic abilities. Sir John Bowring, a British diplomat and governor of Hong Kong, may have known as many as 200 languages.

Such claims are difficult to verify, particularly when they concern historical figures. What counted as knowing a language? Was it familiarity with its vocabulary and grammar, the ability to read and write it, to translate, or to communicate comfortably with native speakers? These are very different levels of linguistic ability.

Fazah’s abilities were put to the test in 1997 on Chilean television. During a live appearance , he was asked basic questions in several languages, including Russian, Greek and Hindi. He struggled to answer correctly, even when asked relatively simple questions. The performance cast serious doubt on his claims, and his name subsequently disappeared from the “Guinness Book of World Records.”
The episode illustrates a crucial distinction: Knowing some of a language is not the same as being fluent in it.

Fluency in a language is not an all-or-nothing achievement. It is a spectrum, ranging from basic conversational ability to sophisticated, near-native command. Someone might understand a language quite well but struggle to speak it. Another person might hold a conversation comfortably but have difficulty reading or writing. Proficiency can vary across the different ways people understand and use a language.

Linguists generally assess language proficiency across several areas, including speaking, listening, reading and writing. These abilities do not necessarily develop at the same rate. A person who can introduce themselves, order a meal and ask for directions may have a useful working knowledge of a language, but that is not the same as being able to debate politics, understand wordplay or conduct professional business in it.

This makes claims about polyglotism particularly difficult to evaluate. There is no simple threshold that determines when someone can legitimately say they speak a language . And counting languages tells us little without knowing the level of proficiency in each.
Not all extraordinary claims are exaggerated.

One remarkable example is Christopher Taylor . A British savant who was born in 1960 and died in 2020, Taylor and his language abilities have long been studied by researchers. Savant syndrome is a rare condition in which someone with a developmental or intellectual disability displays exceptional ability in a particular area, such as music, mathematics or, in Taylor’s case, languages.

Taylor experienced significant developmental delays as a child. As an adult he still required support with everyday activities. Yet he demonstrated an extraordinary capacity for learning languages. He could read, write, translate and converse in 15 to 20 languages, including Danish, Dutch, Finnish, German, Greek, Hindi, Italian, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish and Welsh.

His proficiency varied. In some languages he could hold a conversation; in others his understanding was more basic. But his ability to acquire new linguistic knowledge was remarkable. Much of his learning was self-directed, using introductory language books, dictionaries and interactions with native speakers.

In one experiment , published in 1993, Taylor learned the North African language Berber. Researchers found that he quickly grasped aspects of its complex grammar, including patterns of word order and verb agreement. He also mastered an artificial language called Epun, which researchers had invented specifically for the study. This suggested that his abilities extended beyond memorizing familiar words or phrases.

Taylor’s case is extraordinary, but it also offers a useful reminder: Even exceptional language ability comes in degrees. Researchers found that his proficiency varied considerably across languages. He was fluent in some, while in others he had only a basic knowledge. Being able to demonstrate knowledge of a language in a controlled experiment is not necessarily the same as using it fluently in everyday life.
So is it possible to speak 20, 50 or even 100 languages?

Certainly, people can acquire knowledge of many languages, and some exceptional learners can achieve impressive levels of proficiency across several. But the more languages someone says they speak, the more important it becomes to ask what that claim actually means.

Language is more than a collection of vocabulary and grammatical rules. It involves understanding other people, responding spontaneously, interpreting cultural references and adapting to different social situations. A person may memorize thousands of words without being able to sustain a conversation. And proficiency is not necessarily permanent. Languages can become harder to use when they are not regularly practiced, particularly when someone is maintaining several at once.

Polyglots remind us of the remarkable flexibility of the human mind. But their stories also challenge our assumptions about what it means to know a language. Rather than simply counting tongues, we need to look at what people can actually do with them.

articles.title: Best Side Cycling Tests Out New Henderson Bike Lane in Rainier Beach
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Hanoch of the Youtube channel Best Side Cycling visited an important new protected bike facility in Southeast Seattle, which upgraded safety conditions on the crash-prone corridor of S Henderson Street. The new facility safely connects Be'er Sheva Park and Rainier Beach School in the east to the Chief Sealth Trail farther west, linking destinations like South Shore K-8 school and Rainier Beach Pool and Community Center along the way.

The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) incorporated Toronto-style concrete barriers on much of the facility to make sure the bike lane is truly protected. Road medians and speed cushions also provide traffic calming on the speeding-prone thoroughfare, aiding all people using the street. With trees still in their fall glory, it's a great time to ride the facility. That said, Hanoch gave the sage advice to tread carefully over piles of leaves as they can be very slippery, especially when wet.

South Seattle has generally trailed North Seattle and the downtown core in getting high-quality protected bike lanes, and that has contributed to it seeing far more fatal crashes and serious traffic injuries than other districts of the city. SDOT reported 71 crashes in the Henderson segment alone from 2021 to 2022, as Best Side Cycling noted, underscoring the need for the project.

However, bit by bit , SDOT is pushing to make up the gap, with the safe streets community long pressing for a more equitable distribution of safe facilities across the city – flagging that South Seattle was getting left behind. Though delayed, major bike network upgrades are planned in South Beacon Hill (extending the recently completed North Beacon Hill bike lane ) and Georgetown .

As for the new Henderson facility, Hanoch's review was positive: "I don't mean to just glaze SDOT, but this one I really do feel they're taking a lot of the best practices they've seen in a lot of different places, and we will use them here, like this daylighting in front of those that parking. It's much bigger than some other places like on Union Street."

articles.title: Pikes/Pines | Micro-dramas and bright tail feathers — Capitol Hill’s Dark-eyed Juncos
articles.author: Brendan McGarry
paras: A male Dark-eyed Junco in my parent’s backyard in Seattle. (Image: Brendan McGarry)
As November settles over Capitol Hill and 4:27 PM darkness becomes the daily norm, the neighborhood’s green spaces and parking strips suddenly come alive with low-to-the-ground micro-dramas.

Watching birds in my backyard was my gateway to becoming a birder — they visited our bird feeders, they found food and shelter in my mother’s large garden, they were always doing something interesting if I took the time to pay attention. By far the most ubiquitous species were Dark-eyed Juncos, Junco hyemalis , that showed up in large flocks when fall weather took hold on the Pacific Northwest. Until I became a bit more fluent in the world of birds and our local ecologies, I assumed that they all left for the summer because I didn’t see them for months, until one day I was walking the dog and found a pair of them tirelessly feeding three twittering fledglings in a de facto greenspace adjacent to a local high school. As a fledgling birder, I suddenly realized that things are often more nuanced than flat statements I read in books, and that even common birds have interesting stories to tell.

Dark-eyed Juncos are prettily adorned, small sparrows with dark caps, brown bodies, and eye-catching white outer-tail feathers (this plumage varies a lot by region, but more on that later). But overall they are largely unassuming sparrows that fade into their environment, partially because they also happen to be one of the most abundant birds in North America. Depending on who you ask, their population ranges from 220 million to 630 million. That’s a big variation, but the point is that there are hundreds of millions of juncos across the continent at any one time.
eBird hotspots for Dark-eyed Juncos across the Hill and central Seattle. They are definitely around.

The Hill also has plenty, and you can find juncos just about anywhere with a little bit of greenery, even our most urban blocks. Across the country, and indeed our state, they range from sea level up to the sub-alpine (where they visit to breed and return to moderate climates in winter). Juncos are just about everywhere except extreme deserts, open tundra, and the densest of forests. This ability to roll with a variety of habitats is in part why they remain so abundant despite widespread ecological changes in our world.

Juncos are also birds of the edge lands. They spend their time on the ground or in low shrubs, rarely moving to the tops of trees, except when males fly up high to sing during the breeding season. Food is primarily seeds and other vegetable matter, which they are happy to glean directly from plants, or pick off the ground. Each fall I excitedly wait for the junco flock to return to our yard, flitting in to bend over all the old flower heads of native plants I’ve left to seed. Juncos are around in the summer too, but paired up, on territory, and feeding their young endless invertebrates, shifting their diet to closer to 50/50 plant and vegetable matter.

This shift of food preferences and their breeding behavior are part of the reason I never saw juncos during the summers at my childhood home in North Seattle. Juncos typically nest on or very near the ground, and young leave the nest before they can actually fly because sitting and waiting till they can leaves them vulnerable. We had a dog and an outdoor cat, so despite my mom’s landscaping being quite inviting to juncos, it wasn’t a good place to nest nor for flightless young to roam. Our bird feeders were likewise less attractive to juncos and other birds who focus on the bonanza of insects during warmer months. Besides, the nearby greenspace likely offered more invertebrates because many of our neighbors used insecticides on their landscaping, which are often undiscerning in what insects they target and effectively remove major food sources.
A young Dark-eyed Junco that probably just learned to fly. (Image: Brendan McGarry)

Dark-eyed Juncos may be a common bird, but this abundance and their relatively obliging behavior has made them the star of many studies about North American songbirds. Juncos helped us gain a greater understanding of annual hormonal cycles in birds, offered up good opportunities to study avian dominance and hierarchy structures within flocks, and are even among the species that helped debunk the idea that birds can’t smell. Researchers have demonstrated that juncos can tell each other apart by the scent of the oils they produce in the uropygial gland at the base of their tail. Most birds use oils from this gland when preening, helping waterproof their plumage and likely protecting them from microbial wear. In the case of juncos this also helps them smell each other apart, and even pick a successful, good smelling mate.

We are lucky to have these plucky little birds year-round on the Hill, and their numbers swell right about now, when the juncos who went to breed at higher elevations return to saner wintering grounds. But despite being widespread in North America, some juncos only show up to winter across a large swath of the lower 48 and don’t breed there at all. A lot of people still call them by their old name, Snowbird. And, the birds we call juncos, and those people across the midwest and eastern US might call snowbirds, don’t look entirely identical.
A “Slate-colored Junco,” the bird a lot of people call snowbirds. (Image: USFWS)

Many widespread bird species have sub-populations with very different plumages, body sizes, and even behaviors. Just like Red-tailed Hawks and Song Sparrows – Dark-eyed Juncos have strong geographic variation, particularly noticeable in their coloration. We have “Oregon” Juncos on the Hill and across the Pacific States, while the classic snowbirds of back east are called Slate-colored Juncos (in this situation I guess Oregon means more brown). The variety of junco plumages flummoxed early taxonomists and at one point ornithologists considered today’s Dark-eyed Juncos to be five different species until genetic work demonstrated low variation between populations. Across their range juncos are still mostly doing junco things – spending time on the ground, with similar vocalizations, and eating a lot of seeds.

Despite these similarities and ornithologists’ choice to call Dark-eyed Juncos a single species, recent research suggests that we are witnessing the beginning of a rapid speciation within the genus Junco . Dark-eyed Juncos appear to have expanded into North America after the last ice age, likely speciating from a related species that lives in the mountains of Southern Arizona, New Mexico, and Mexico, the Yellow-eyed Junco, Junco phaeonotus . Under this context, the difference in color, migration patterns, body size, and overall behavior that we see in different Dark-eyed Junco populations across North America is quite exciting (at least to ornithologists, evolutionary biologists, and me), and has happened quite fast – most vertebrates don’t speciate over the course of ten thousand years.
A fun image of extant Junco species and Dark-eyed Junco subspecies, across North and Central America from the Lab of Borja Milá at Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales in Madrid, Spain .

Though I appreciate all the various things Dark-eyed Juncos might represent to science, I don’t necessarily need all that to appreciate them. I love when I get a calm moment and can sit still and watch them work through the yard – I witness micro-dramas over food, hear their near constant vocalizations from muttered twitters to emphatic clicks, and when something scares up the flock, the garden is awash in flashes of their white outer tail feathers. Every winter I also wait for that first trilling song, because Dark-eyed Juncos are one of the first birds to begin singing in earnest as the days lengthen. Even now, as I find myself in near darkness at 5pm, I am warmed by the idea of a junco soon to be singing from the top of a tree.

articles.title: Sound Transit Funds Study to Speed Up D Line Bus
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Thursday, the Sound Transit Board allocated $500,000 to fund a study of bus speed and reliability improvements for the RapidRide D Line, which runs from Downtown Seattle to Ballard and Crown Hill. It's an early signal that D Line riders can expect a faster ride – a few years down the road, anyway.

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay brought forward the budget amendment, with support from Tukwila Mayor Thomas McLeod and the entire Seattle delegation on the agency board: Mayor Katie Wilson, City Councilmember Dan Strauss, and County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda.

A timeline for the project was not immediately clear, but supporters noted it was important to provide interim improvements while Ballard and Interbay wait on its delayed light rail project. In 2016, the campaign for the successful Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure pledged to deliver Ballard Link by 2035, but the timeline has slipped since then.

“I’m very, very happy to be sponsoring this amendment, bringing half a million dollars forward, so that Sound Transit and the City and King County can together work to advance the planning and improve the RapidRide D to Ballard," Wilson said. "We know that that’s no substitute for light rail, but right now it is the third busiest route in King County. It carries more than 10,000 riders a day, and making this bus work better will ease the mobility burden in this regional growth center and keep people moving while we do that longer term work.”

Zahilay credited the Save Ballard Rail coalition with raising the need for D Line improvements. Designing the project will entail a collaboration between Sound Transit, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), and King County Metro. While Metro operates the bus, SDOT maintains the roadway over which it runs, and the Seattle Transit Measure also funds extra service that boosts bus frequency.

"I want to specifically thank Save Ballard Rail, who has been regularly in touch with my staff and asked us to look into ways to expedite improvements to the RapidRide D line," Zahilay said. "This amendment would move $500,000 of already committed funding for this project up to 2027 to ensure that Sound Transit, SDOT, and Metro explore options and start planning for these capital improvements that would be intended to speed up the RapidRide D."

Zahilay reminded the board that ST3 included funding for Seattle bus improvements as an early deliverable . Namely, it included $35 million to "design and implement transit priority improvements along King County Metro’s RapidRide C and D lines that provide service to Ballard and West Seattle as an early deliverable to provide improved speed and reliability, in advance of light rail starting operations to these areas."

"When voters approved Sound Transit 3, they approved a modest amount of funding to advance the RapidRide D resources for capital improvements, bus and traffic signal priority, just to help move people in the interim while the light rail station and light rail was getting to Ballard," Zahilay said.

That funding was a victim of the 2021 realignment vote , which delayed a number of projects due to pandemic-related planning delays and budgetary strain. The early deliverable went from an early deliverable to a late deliverable without a definite timeline.

"This was originally designed to be an early deliverable in 2025, but in 2021, the board voted to delay the timeline as part of a realignment plan, and I want to speed things back up again," Zahilay said. "I think this board has made it clear that getting to Market Street in the long term, as the CEO mentioned, is a priority for this board. And we have also said that, in the short term, we want to improve transit service in that area through transit mitigation efforts."

As it stands, Sound Transit's best-case scenario for light rail to reach Ballard is 2042 – although the agency has granted that many hurdles remain and has not ruled out the opening date slipping to the 2060s if those hurdles are not navigated.
Jonatan Gonzalez, an organizer with Save Ballard Rail, spoke in favor of the amendment at Thursday's board meeting.
"As we know, Ballard is waiting for light rail, and we can improve bus service now," Gonzalez said. "That'd be amazing."
Metro spokesperson Jeff Switzer told The Urbanist that Metro, in partnership with SDOT and Sound Transit, had some earlier planning to build upon, but that those concepts would need updating.

"Following voter approval of this investment in 2016, work began to identify projects that would improve speed and reliability along the corridor," Switzer said. "That effort was paused following the initial realignment process, and Metro plans to update the analysis to identify RapidRide D enhancements that can be delivered in the near term for the benefit of riders."

Wilson and Zahilay both emphasized bus improvements in their successful runs in 2025. Zahilay reiterated that accelerating the R Line project , replacing Route 7 in the Rainier Valley, was a priority for his administration, and recently cleared a King County Council committee approval vote .

One of Wilson's signature moves in her first year, meanwhile, was rapidly rolling out a bus lane for Route 8. Long notorious for its lateness, Route 8 has since seen a dramatic jump in speed and reliability thanks to the street redesign, a project her predecessor, Bruce Harrell, had sought to frame as completely infeasible.

The same style treatment for the D Line could result in huge time savings for riders. The route lacks consistent bus lanes outside of downtown, with SDOT offering brief sections a few blocks at a time rather than a connected treatment.

Another big move for Wilson was a renewal proposal that doubled the size of the Seattle Transit Measure, which will provide funding to boost frequencies on about a dozen bus lines , with the D a likely candidate. The transit measure passed resoundingly in November with more than 72% of the vote.

With the D Line study just now getting off the ground, the scope of the project is not yet clear. Strauss floated the idea of an express bus with reduced stops shadowing the route. He also underscored how slow the bus is now.

"I will state: that RapidRide is very slow," Strauss said. "It is a milk-run bus out to Ballard going through Uptown. Its travel times are 40 to 45 minutes from where you sit right now just to downtown Ballard."
As riders reacted to the news, some disputed the trip times Strauss has quoted as exagerrated.

"Why does he feel the need to pad everything? It's 27 to 36 minutes from Pioneer Square to Market Street depending on time of day," Seattle Transit Blog contributor David Lawson wrote in a Bluesky post . "Lots of room for improvement, but the work that's already been done has made a difference."

One joked that Strauss did not know what a milk run is, alluding to the D's straight rather than circuitous routing. On the other hand, another D Line rider noted reliability and bus bunching issues can add wait times at stops.

Strauss has mentioned on multiple occasions that he thinks the routing through Uptown to serve Seattle Center slows the route down too much. The drawback would be that skipping the Seattle Center would decrease Northwest Seattle's access to that popular destination, and it may require shifting another route over to provide adequate coverage for Uptown.
One way or the other, improvements appear inbound, although just how dramatic and imminent is yet to be determined.

"The RapidRide D Line serves 10,500 riders on an average weekday and is the third busiest route in the region. It provides critical connections between Ballard, Interbay, Uptown, and Downtown Seattle, while also linking customers to other frequent transit services throughout the city," Switzer said. "We look forward to partnering with Sound Transit and SDOT to advance improvements that enhance reliability, speed, and the overall customer experience on this important corridor."

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Sound Transit Bingo
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To celebrate 30 years since voters passed Sound Move , Sound Transit is hosting a transit Bingo game today. Sound Move was the Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority’s first voter approved funding package to build a regional transit system. The Sound Transit brand was not adopted until 1997. Sound Move included commuter rail between Everett-Seattle and Lakewood-Seattle, light rail in Tacoma and between Seattle-SeaTac, and an extensive network of express buses in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties.

The first component of Sound Move to enter service, ST Express, began on September 19, 1999 with nine routes. Commuter rail service started the following year with trips between Seattle and Tacoma. The agency’s first light rail line, then-called Tacoma Link, opened in August 2003. Light rail service in Seattle, Central Link, began service on July 18, 2009 between downtown Seattle and Tukwila.

Everyone is invited to explore the region while visiting stations to fill in their Bingo card today between 10am to 2pm. The first 450 people to complete a row, column, or diagonal and return their card to a designated drop-off will get a 30th Anniversary ORCA card . Everyone who gets Bingo will be entered into a raffle to win additional prizes. If you want to go above and beyond, complete every square for a chance to win a grand prize that includes one year of free transit and a behind-the-scenes ride-along through a Link train wash. For more details and the complete list of prizes, visit the Sound Transit website .

articles.title: Jackson Street Housing Project Could Leave King County on Hook for Millions
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A proposal from King County Executive Girmay Zahilay to finance an affordable housing project is raising some eyebrows at the County Council, due to a draft lease agreement that could leave the County's general fund on the hook for unexpected cost increases for years down the line. The project, at 701 S Jackson Street in Seattle's Chinatown-International District (CID), would include 111 new, mostly family-sized units along with retail space but also turn King County into a tenant charged with paying off bonds used for building construction.

The ordinance currently in front of the County Council would provide financing to a $63.8 million apartment building that has been stalled for many years. Developers Nitze-Stagen and the Housing Diversity Corporation, operating as a joint entity called O.Z. Navigator, secured permits for 701 S Jackson Street in 2022 as a 238-unit building, mostly one-bedroom units and studios.

Going in on a site previously owned by the CID's storied Mar family, the former gas station required significant site remediation work to make it suitable for housing. And even though that remediation work is now complete, the construction project was never able to move forward due to financing issues.

Six years later, the project has been redesigned with far more family-sized units, making it more attractive to public financers following an oversaturation of Seattle's studio and one-bedroom affordable housing market. Of 111 total apartments, 96 would be two-bedrooms, and 14 would be three-bedroom, all available to residents making 67% of King County's area median income or below – around $90,000 per year for a family of three. Designs include one one-bedroom unit.

Included in a slate of housing investments tucked into Zahilay's proposed mid-biennial budget update this fall, the 701 S Jackson project was notable in that it was missing a specific dollar commitment, in contrast with line items like a $4 million earmark for the Pacific Tower Quarters Building in Beacon Hill and $1.8 million for a veteran's housing project in Kirkland.
That's because the deal in the International District would be structured very differently than the other projects.

Under the ordinance that could be voted on as soon as December 8, King County would serve as the third party on a Development Services Agreement with the Housing Diversity Corporation and a nonprofit specifically set up for the project, 701 Essential Housing. That entity would issue up to $90 million in tax-exempt bonds to build the project, with Housing Diversity Corporation the developer.

"Upon completion of construction, the Master Lease Agreement would be effective, allowing the County to lease the property from 701 Essential Housing," a staff report from late October noted. "On behalf of the County, 701 Essential Housing would manage subleases for residential and retail tenants. The County would make payments to 701 Essential Housing to cover any remaining debt service and operations costs not covered by sublease revenue. At the end of the 30-year lease term and full repayment of the bonds, the County would assume ownership of the property."

In the financial scenario envisioned by Zahilay's office, the County would be responsible for paying $37.5 million over the life of the project, with a maximum annual payment of around $2.5 million in 2032 that ramps down over time.

King County Chief Budget Officer Aaron Rubardt told councilmembers that the County's general fund, under significant strain in recent years by restrictions on property tax growth and limited growth in unincorporated areas outside cities, is currently tabbed as the primary source of revenue for the project. But Rubardt also noted that another funding source could be found at a later time – potentially the countywide housing levy that Zahilay has been formally considering since shortly after taking office.

"The proposal is for the general fund to back this, and we built into our general fund projections that the general fund would pay the debt service," Rubardt told councilmembers. "But over time, the Executive and Council can make a decision to have another funding source fund it. So I think that is fungible over time. So keep that in mind, it doesn't all have to be paid by the general fund, but the obligation that we're signing up for does obligate the general fund as the backer of the debt."

A $37.5 million general fund contribution to fund 111 units would amount to one of the largest set-asides for an individual affordable housing project in King County history. The proposed investment works out to just over $337,000 per unit, albeit spaced out over 30 years.

In 2025, King County’s Housing Finance Program awarded $23.7 million to eight projects total, helping to advance a collective total of 672 homes – however, all of those projects were receiving additional financing on top of any County contribution.

But as laid out in staff analysis presented during Tuesday's work session, the county's contribution isn't fixed in place. Various scenarios could play out that would balloon that number, including lower-than-expected occupancy of the rental units, increased construction costs, and higher interest rates.

With a 30% increase in project costs, the staff presentation noted, the County contribution could end up at $77.2 million, doubling the amount in projected pro-forma plan that the Zahilay administration presented. With a 1% more expensive bond coupon, costs could go up by $20 million. A vacancy rate at 701 S Jackson Street that is double what's currently expected could cost the County an additional $13 million, despite the fact that the County would not be in control of managing the rentals itself.
Even more worrying for the general fund is the fact that these scenarios could all occur to various degrees, with nothing constraining the top cost that the County would be held responsible for.
"It is not possible to predict which of these scenarios, or which combination, might occur," this week's updated staff report noted.

During the meeting, Rubardt faced questions about why the deal was structured in this specific way, with Rubardt pointing to the need to stand up affordable units quickly. A slowdown in development traced to higher interest rates and higher operating costs for existing affordable housing buildings does mean that there are fewer shovel-ready projects that the County could plug itself into.

"The priority was for 111 family-sized units in the International District, two bedrooms and three bedrooms," Rubardt said. "The reason we are proposing this now under this arrangement is that we think it's a fast way, a relatively fast way, to get something built and to open up those affordable housing units, so we can have them open in 2029, hopefully."
Executive's Office spokesperson Callie Craighead provided additional information about Zahilay's decision to turn to this type of lease agreement in a follow-up email to The Urbanist .

"This is a new financing model for the County for funding affordable housing; however, it is not new to the county," Craighead wrote. "King County has used this financing model for other buildings, including office buildings in the downtown office core. This financing model has also been used by local universities to fund dormitories. The County is looking for innovative ways to finance urgent housing needs. "

"This funding arrangement provided the flexibility to fund affordable housing relatively quickly; and at the end of agreement the County will have acquired both the land and facility," Craighead added.

In the rosy scenario, that transfer could provide the County an asset that could operate at a profit, generating a revenue stream for additional public investments in housing or otherwise. In the not-so-rosy scenario, the County could inherit an aging building with a maintenance backlog for which it would continue to be on the hook.

Though Zahilay's office is pushing for a vote on the agreement before the end of 2026, Tuesday's meeting was the first substantive conversation to occur on the proposal at the council level – an October 28 briefing was cancelled due to other agenda items running long.
During the recent work session, several councilmembers raised clear concerns about exposing the general fund to this level of unexpected cost increases.

"I think I heard that it would be difficult for us to legislate to share that risk differently," Councilmember Claudia Balducci said. "Although I would recommend that we try, because you know, if we're taking all of the risk, that's a tough ask for the County's general fund."
Craighead defended Zahilay's approach to managing King County's finances.

"The Executive always scrutinizes allocating limited General Fund dollars and limiting the fiscal risk to the County," Craighead wrote. "As part of his commitment to building a better government, Executive Zahilay’s proposed second omnibus budget maintains the General Fund’s emergency reserves at 8% and the 'rainy day fund.' The Executive and the Budget Team is starting to work through scenario planning for the 2028-2029 budget to minimize risk and deliver a balanced budget."

Following the work session, the council held a closed-door discussion of the legal risks behind the deal, a session held at the request of Councilmember Jorge Barón. If the ordinance is rejected, that would represent the biggest break between Zahilay's office and the County Council so far during his term, with the council largely deferring to Executive branch priorities so far.
On the other hand, it's possible that the council is able to come around to Zahilay's proposal, potentially by putting additional guardrails on the lease agreement.
Balducci noted that if the general fund ends up getting tapped more than expected to meet the County's obligations, that could lead to service cuts elsewhere in County government.
"People lose their jobs, and we end up cutting vital services," Balducci said. "So, I just think we need to be very clear about what risk we're taking on and how good or bad we feel about that."

articles.title: Tacoma Council Axes Crisis Response Team, Slashes City Budget to Address Deficit
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: Facing a major fiscal cliff to the tune of $40 million over the next biennium, the City of Tacoma was forced to make sharp cuts to its 2027-2028 biennial budget, which the Tacoma City Council adopted in a unanimous vote Tuesday.

These cuts included eliminating more than 100 staff positions, 14 of which were filled, as well as cutting the City’s fairly new civilian co-responder Holistic Outreach Promoting Engagement (HOPE) team, and whittling down the police department’s community service officer (CSO) team.

Even though these cost-saving measures reduced the City’s 2027-2028 deficit back down to zero, this doesn’t mean that Tacoma is in the clear for the long term. The City still projects an $18 million budget shortfall by the time the next biennial budget rolls around. By the 2031-2032 biennium, the City will once again face a $40 million shortfall.

Public reaction to the decision to cut the HOPE Team, a program through the Tacoma Fire Department, was especially negative. Several members of the public, including a number of community activists and a representative from the NAACP, called for its retention and for the City to revisit how it dispatched the team. At least one member of the public said that they felt like the city was breaking the promise it had made in the wake of Manuel Ellis’s death in custody of Tacoma police officers in March 2020.

But civilian crisis response is not permanently off the table. The City introduced two amendments that put $150,000 towards a crisis response study and $400,000 toward crisis response and case management support. The latter amendment is meant as a bridge to sustain some capacity for crisis response between HOPE’s elimination and whatever team may replace it. The HOPE team had been budgeted at $4 million over the next two years before the cuts.

The city will also retain five of the 10 total community service officer positions through the Tacoma Police Department. These officers handle non-emergency calls. The City had initially considered entirely eliminating this cohort of officers.
“For years,” a slide in the city’s Oct. 27 budget presentation reads, “the cost of running the City has grown almost twice as fast as the money it collects.”

At that meeting — which served as the first hearing for the proposed biennial budget — the City’s finance director, Andy Cherullo, told councilmembers that the City had been facing a $40 million structural deficit in the General Fund. Without the proposed cuts, he continued, the structural deficit would grow to $75 million by the 2029-2030 biennium, and $106 million by the 2031-2032 biennium.
But this doesn’t mean the City is out of the woods.
“We are still projecting structural deficits in the next couple of biennium,” Cherullo said. “There are further hard decisions in the future for this City Council.”
The impending budget shortfall isn’t for lack of trying — and it isn’t an unfamiliar problem.
State law limits how quickly some revenues can grow. For instance, property tax levies can only grow at a rate of 1% per year.

“There’s no City expense that grows at 1% per year,” Cherullo said. “Just like our community members, the City is not immune to the higher inflation currently in the economy. We are also facing higher costs for fuel, supplies, and services. Benefits like health care are growing at double-digit rates, and there's general uncertainty related to what direction the overall economy will move that can impact other City revenues like sales tax and our business and occupation taxes.”
There is also an increasing demand for City services, and wages, benefits, and supplies cost more every year.
Together, this all creates a difficult situation for the City.

“Unless the state gives us more opportunities to have progressive revenue sources at the local level, we’re going to continue to have these problems year after year after year, and it’s been happening for the last 24 years,” Deputy Mayor Joe Bushnell said at the council’s Nov. 10 meeting. “So people are wondering, ‘Well why can’t the City be creative about these different things?’ It’s because we are struggling to fund basic services as it is. We can’t be as creative as we’d like to be because we don’t have the revenue sources or the options available to us from beyond our powers here.”
In passing the budget, Bushnell was also the only member of the council to acknowledge that the City had cut staffed positions.

“I […] want to recognize that through this budget, we eliminated 100 positions, and behind many of those positions were people, great dedicated staff doing amazing work on behalf of our community,” he said at the Nov. 17 meeting. “A hundred positions have been eliminated out of this budget, and I just don’t want us to lose sight of that fact, because that’s not actually a good thing, I think, for our city, because those are services that are not going to be rendered.”

City Manager Hyun Kim told The Urbanist in a later interview that cutting the 14 filled positions was not an easy decision, and that the City’s Human Resources worked hard to identify where it could keep staff whose positions were originally going to be cut. Prior to budget deliberations, a little more than half of identified positions were filled.

“[W]e got that number down to 14. […] We really did try our best to give as much advance notice to our employees that are impacted employees in those filled positions and that's why we gave the notice, we gave options,” Kim said. “We were not completely successful because as was mentioned last night by our deputy mayor, there's a human story here. We've got 14 individuals that will receive layoff notices in the coming days. It's one of the hardest things that I have to do in this job.”

In a later interview, Mayor Anders Ibsen told The Urbanist that, for the last several months, he has been having discussions with lawmakers and leaders from other jurisdictions about new legislation that could allow jurisdictions to find new sources of revenue and break out of the restrictive revenue-sourcing cycle that repeatedly forces them into difficult budget cycles.

Ibsen said that the state may be facing severe budget challenges, but that isn’t just due to the economy. It’s also because of the state’s limited tax code. In many ways, he said, that sets local communities up to fail “because we have revenue sources that are always going to decline relative to inflation. That's why we're always in cut situations. That's not sustainable or fair, and it needs to change.”

“What you're going to see cities like Tacoma push for in the legislative session […] as the legislature approaches the tax code, is to make sure we don't have a two-tiered system where the state passes unfunded mandates down to us [which] gives us local taxing options,” Ibsen said. “We don't want to just continue having local taxing options. We want to have tools, but we also want to make sure that we have a unified tax code that is a shared burden for funding core services like public education, public safety, homelessness, you name it. It has to be a shared approach rather than robbing Peter to pay Paul.”
The city initially created the five-person HOPE Team three years ago, following the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests and the death of Manuel Ellis in Tacoma police custody in 2020.

In justifying cutting the team, the City appeared to suggest that the HOPE Team had been underutilized in its three years in existence. A slide from the council’s Oct. 27 meeting states that the HOPE Team answered about three calls per day in 2026, that it was hard to staff, and that the team was only available for limited hours. City policy also requires police officers or firefighters on the scene for safety reasons.
The Tacoma Fire Department also initially put out an Oct. 27 joint press release with the Tacoma Police Department explaining the pending cuts of the HOPE and CSO teams.

Though both departments pulled the press release shortly after its publication, the departments stated in that press release that both teams had “struggled to maintain intended staffing levels and have never been adequately positioned to effectively serve the community” from the get-go. The departments said that the teams responded to just a “fraction” of service calls the department received.

“One of the primary goals of HOPE was to relieve traditional first responders to focus their duty on calls where behavioral health issues were not the primary need for service,” the joint press release stated. “In many cases, HOPE and CSO efforts have proven redundant. Nearly all HOPE responses, for example, have also required the presence of paramedics, police officers, or firefighters. In reality, 99% of HOPE requests have required traditional first responder co-response since July 2023.”

But several members of the public argued that the HOPE Team — at barely three years old, with no studies showing its efficacy or lack thereof — was hardly getting a fair hearing, and that the City was cutting it prematurely.

“It’s accurate when everybody says that HOPE has been underfunded, understaffed, and underutilized, and I want to tell you that that is, in fact, your fault,” said Jonathan Pottle at the council’s Oct. 27 meeting. “Axing the HOPE Team is not an operational necessity. It’s an ideological choice, and it is a bad one.”

Both Theresa Power-Drutis, a longtime community organizer who works as the director of the New Connections re-entry program, and Barb Church, an environmental and community activist, told councilmembers that they needed to reconsider the way the HOPE Team is dispatched and accessible, rather than just eliminate it.

“If the team is eliminated, what happens? Police or fire will transport those in crisis to emergency rooms or shelters or jail. … However, shelters, jails, and emergency rooms do not provide resources for long-term mental health recovery,” added Calista Brown, another member of the public.

Like Power-Drutis and Church, Brown also suggested that the city “consider creative ways to enable HOPE’s operating at the capacity that truly meets community needs” and “how to offset ongoing understaffing, how to institute independent deployment.” She also highlighted that “police and fire have required co-response shutting down direct community access.”
“Review all the data that HOPE has collected so that the how and why of HOPE's effectiveness informs your decision to keep, eliminate, or truncate it,” Brown said.

“We have heard police officers say repeatedly that they are not trained to respond to mental health crises. […] A number of Tacoma police officers have described the HOPE Team as beneficial and stated they would like to see the HOPE Team expanded into late-night hours to be able to provide more extended support,” said Julie Andrzejewski, the co-chair of Indivisible Tacoma. “It's a cost-effective service. Eliminating it will result in greater costs, both human and financial.”

Gemini, a member of Tacoma Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression, seconded several other pro-HOPE commenters, and likewise underscored that the team didn’t even get a fighting chance. They also reminded the city of the financial cost of having no crisis responders.

“It’s kind of callous to talk about saving people's lives in the measure of dollars, but I understand we’re talking about a budget,” Gemini said. “I think we really need to think about how much money is spent when the police are dispatched to these crises. How much money was spent when SWAT was sent to Rhoda Butler’s house and shot her down and killed her? How much did that cost the city? How much did it cost the city to defend Manny Ellis’s murderers and pay out those murderers for the tunes of millions of dollars? […] We need to be weighing the real cost of police violence and [ … ] institutional violence against how much the HOPE Team costs, even if it was fully funded.”

During public comment at the council’s Nov. 10 meeting, Tacoma community member Nikki SnowKing member of the public who identified herself as Nikki reminded the council that it had made “an explicit promise to this community in the wake of Black Lives Matter and a call for accountability.”

“We were promised that Tacoma would fundamentally change its approach to public safety. You promised to invest in human-centered, non-police responses that protect rather than endanger our most vulnerable community members,” Nikki said. “The HOPE program is a direct realization of these promises. […] Dismantling the program is a clear retreat from the commitments that were made in Manuel Ellis’ name and to the Black and vulnerable communities of Tacoma.”

Ibsen told The Urbanist that “the promise that the city made was to keep Tacoma safe, while also partnering with the community to build on that trust, and the key behind that isn't the programs, it's the essence of what we're doing.”

articles.title: Thanks to new generation of office space, Capitol Hill’s daytime population ranges from Duolingo to start-ups
articles.author: CHS
paras: CENTRL Office’s Capitol Hill Location (Image: Matt Freire)
Building out a traditional office on Capitol Hill comes with real overhead — even for small upgrades.

According to City of Seattle construction permits signed off this month, language-learning giant Duolingo spent a base $18,000 on interior alterations just to add a dedicated lactation room inside its fifth-floor offices inside the net-zero energy Bullitt Center at 15th and Madison

While established companies can absorb bespoke buildouts and permitting timelines, Capitol Hill’s smaller office rentals and coworking spaces are giving homegrown entrepreneurs an affordable alternative, offering shared amenities and flexible footprints without the upfront capital expense.

As remote and hybrid work spaces reshape how businesses utilize office space, coworking and office rentals are seeing an increased interest from freelancers and small teams, according to the developers behind the spaces.

While overall Seattle office vacancy remained elevated at 27.7% in Q3 2026, it has begun edging down from its peak and neighborhood submarkets are faring substantially better than the downtown core, according to commercial real estate firm Kidder Mathews . In the Capitol Hill and Central District submarket, total vacancy stood at 10.5% across 4.8 million square feet of inventory, compared to 35% downtown. Locally, Capitol Hill’s CENTRL Office reported a 30% increase in occupancy over the past year.
Kaitee Quinn , general manager at CENTRL, said that these environments are becoming an essential stepping stone in business growth today.

“I think we’re filling a need that has been created by everybody preferring remote and hybrid work now,” Quinn said. “You get to choose to come to a space that’s beautiful, that’s lively, and meet people in your neighborhood.”

Duolingo’s own Capitol Hill footprint followed that trajectory. Before signing its direct lease at the Bullitt Center, the company’s Seattle team operated out of coworking desks inside the historic Kelly-Springfield building on 11th Ave — the same space CENTRL Office now operates.

As regulatory and operating costs rise across the city, these smaller office rentals and coworking spaces give entrepreneurial companies the traditional workplace benefits without having to front the operational expenses.

Different from coworking spaces, the Ballou Wright building on 12th Avenue offers separate office leases for businesses looking for a more traditional workplace. Jill Cronauer, president of Hunters Capital, which owns and manages the Ballou Wright building, said that these spaces are becoming the cost-effective option for small teams.

“There’s a huge distinction about small office space that’s super critical because it’s more affordable,” Cronauer said. “It’s also acting as an essential step down if an organization is resizing and downsizing.”

Cronauer also highlighted the importance of Capitol Hill’s creative atmosphere and access to mass transit as attractive features for businesses. The Ballou Wright building houses many independent tenants, such as marketers, interior designers and architecture firms.

Liz Dunn , developer of The Cloud Room and Chophouse Row , said the coworking space has become a launching pad for many independent businesses, some of which she said eventually grow beyond what the space can provide.

“We always have noticed and love the fact that we have been able to incubate little companies that have then gone on to grow,” Dunn said. “Sometimes we are able to incubate a Cloud Room member company into a user of a different office space at Chophouse. It gives us enormous satisfaction to play that role.”

Locally, shared workspaces have served as launchpads for Seattle’s startups and small businesses. On Capitol Hill, food and drink entrepreneur Makini Howell moved her administrative team into The Cloud Room, where she collaborated with fellow tenant and graphic design studio Wildern on the brand’s identity. Meanwhile, spaces like Foundations on Boylston and CENTRL Office on 11th host dozens of early-stage technical founders. Across the city, coworking hubs and incubators including The Pioneer Collective, 9Zero, AI House , and Waterfront Workspaces have helped launch notable local ventures ranging from screen-free kids’ phone maker Tin Can and proptech startup YIMBY AI to applied-AI companies Lexion, Yoodli, and Vercept .

Some of these offices offer amenities like large meeting rooms, private phone booths, Wi-Fi and coffee in their memberships, which cuts a lot of the overhead costs associated with a traditional office building.
For larger employers, taking on traditional commercial leases and custom tenant improvements remains standard practice.

Pittsburgh-based Duolingo, which employs roughly 900 people globally and operates a regional engineering and product outpost of a few dozen staffers in Capitol Hill, signed a lease in 2024 for 7,940 square feet of office space inside the six-story Bullitt Center. Leasing an entire floorplate in one of the neighborhood’s signature commercial buildings gives the publicly traded edtech company room to customize its own workspace — while underscoring the gap between institutional tech tenants and the solo founders or small teams turning to shared spaces to avoid buildout costs.
In addition to providing independent businesses support, Dunn also said that office space plays an important role for the economy and the identity of the neighborhood.
“A truly successful 24/7 neighborhood has to have residents, retail, and office,” Dunn said. “And I wish we had more office space on Capitol Hill than we do.”
